topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: The entire offset model follows from Kafka keeping the broker stateless and pushing all consumption bookkeeping onto the client
because: The original design pushed all per-consumer state off the broker and onto the client, which is what let Kafka collapse a consumer's progress into one integer; that same collapse is what forces the API to distinguish the read position from the committed position and to insist you commit the next offset rather than the last one, since a single number can't represent 'processed' and 'safe to resume from' separately unless the convention pins down exactly which one it means.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: auto.offset.reset is not a one-time startup choice; it re-fires later, invisibly, whenever a committed offset stops being usable
because: The setting only activates when there is no usable committed offset, but that condition doesn't just occur at first launch -- offsets.retention.minutes can expire an old commit for a low-traffic group, or a group can be mistaken for new -- so the same two-value choice made once, deliberately, at setup time can later trigger unannounced, on its own schedule, as either a mass replay or a silent multi-message loss, and the operator who set it may never be the one present when it fires.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Everything about how a consumer group divides and reassigns work is downstream of one invariant: a partition is owned by exactly one member of a group at a time
because: That single exclusivity rule is what makes scaling past partition count a wasted consumer, what per-topic assignor math can turn into a lopsided split across multiple topics, and what a reader has to run forward by hand to predict correctly under churn; assign() is included as the boundary case, since it is the literal switch that turns this entire coordinated-division apparatus off for a given consumer.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: The classic protocol's synchronous join/sync handshake is what makes a rebalance a full-group pause, not just a housekeeping event for the member that changed
because: The RPC design -- every member must rejoin, only the elected leader computes assignment, and a new generation ID invalidates anyone still on the old one -- is inherited from the earliest ZooKeeper-registration design and is the actual mechanism behind why any single trigger (a join, a leave, a topic change) stops every member in the group, not only the one whose membership changed.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Two separate fixes attack the same synchronous-barrier problem from opposite ends: shrink what a rebalance revokes, or remove the client-side computation step entirely
because: KIP-429 keeps the barrier but adds an owned-partitions field so only genuinely-moving partitions get revoked across a second, smaller round; KIP-848 removes the barrier altogether by making assignment a server-computed, independently-reconciled target state; group.protocol is the literal switch between an old-era client that fully participates in the barrier and a new-era client that does not.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Kafka has two independent liveness signals -- heartbeats and poll() calls -- and nearly every rebalance-tuning setting here is really an argument about how long to trust silence on one of them before assuming the member is dead
because: session.timeout.ms/heartbeat.interval.ms governs the heartbeat signal, while max.poll.interval.ms and max.poll.records govern the poll() signal, and a consumer stuck processing can keep the first alive while going silent on the second -- that split is what makes livelock a distinct failure mode from a crashed process, what makes static membership's tradeoff (accept slower failure detection to survive a restart) a deliberate move on the same axis, and what turned a load-test session-timeout wave into a rebalance storm that never settled.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: A partition-level stall is invisible on every signal except per-partition lag, and in this row set lag itself is only defined inside a hands-on lab rather than as a documented concept
because: A bad deserializer or a slow handler doesn't crash the consumer or show up group-wide -- it just stops one partition's CURRENT-OFFSET from closing the gap to LOG-END-OFFSET while every other partition reads clean -- but the row that actually defines CURRENT-OFFSET and LOG-END-OFFSET only exists because an exercise walked someone through reading them off a CLI, meaning a reader who never runs the lab has no vocabulary for the exact symptom the poison-pill and livelock rows describe.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: At-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once are not three settings to pick between; they are one axis -- when the offset commit happens relative to processing -- read at different points
because: Whether a crash produces loss or a duplicate is decided entirely by which side of the processing step the commit lands on, so auto-commit's fixed timer losing unprocessed records, a manual commit racing a side effect that already fired, and the fact that even disciplined manual commit ordering can't close the duplicate window are the same mechanism observed from three different failure angles, not three unrelated bugs.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Manual commit APIs and the rebalance-revoke callback exist to answer the same question from two directions: how do you commit work Kafka doesn't know is unfinished, before Kafka takes the partition away
because: The client's lack of thread-safety is what forces decoupled processing to route commits back through the single-threaded consumer rather than committing from a worker thread directly; the sync/async split then trades that discipline for throughput in steady state; and the revoke callback is the one moment manual code gets a guaranteed last chance to commit before ownership actually moves, which is exactly why practitioners reach for the blocking call there and nowhere else in the loop.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: A read_committed consumer isn't buffering or filtering messages itself -- it is gating delivery on control markers the transaction coordinator writes to the partition, and that single mechanism explains three separate symptoms
because: The coordinator writing a COMMIT or ABORT marker to every participating partition is what produces the offset gaps a naive consecutive-offset check would misread as loss, what makes a hung transaction able to stall consumption indefinitely until transaction.timeout.ms forces it closed, and what makes read_committed leave ordinary non-transactional writes completely untouched, since markers only exist where a transaction touched the partition.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Every constraint enable.idempotence enforces on other producer settings is a direct requirement of the PID-plus-sequence-number check the broker actually runs, and that same check draws the boundary on what idempotence can and can't deduplicate
because: The broker only accepts a write whose sequence number is exactly one more than the last one it saw for that (PID, partition) pair, which is why in-flight requests must stay boundable, why retries must stay on, and why acks=all is non-negotiable -- the ack has to reflect the write the sequence check just validated; the same per-session, per-partition scope is also why a producer restart resets the count and reopens the door to cross-restart duplicates idempotence was never meant to catch.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
principle: Kafka's exactly-once machinery only ever deduplicates a write to a Kafka partition, so the practical guarantee for any real pipeline is bounded by the last Kafka-internal write, and everything past that point falls back on the same idempotent-consumer discipline at-least-once always required
because: transactional.id is what makes a producer's identity durable across restarts so the boundary itself can be recovered and fenced, and the required producer-plus-consumer combination is what extends that boundary as far as the consumer's own commit -- but a database write, an API call, or any effect outside Kafka sits past the boundary regardless, which is the exact gap the two drills are built to make someone locate by hand rather than assume away.
